notes.role_generic: Questions are role-generic and world-generic. Representatives handle per-world variation; a question meeting a thin record produces an honest calibrated answer. Do NOT add per-world question variants - that matrix was cancelled 2026-07-16.
notes.walk_order: Each set is a walk, not a menu. `order` is the default sequence, each question a natural next step from the last. The participant may jump to any question; the order is a default, not a track.
notes.invariance: All 20 sets stay reachable to every role behind a 'show me everything' affordance. `role` determines what is offered FIRST, never what is reachable. Do not gate on role.
notes.q1_hard_rule: `world_framed: true` is mandatory on every question with order 1. A starter is turn zero and the relational-safety classifier's gentlest category has no prior transcript to anchor to, so first-person present-tense distress phrasing reads as a real disclosure and triages the participant for accepting our own invitation. Tested live; it happened. Enforce in CI if these ever become code.
notes.role_ids: Match the Representative Modes contract (role_modes.py VALID_ROLES). `reevaluation` is the participant-facing rename of `deconstructing`, decided 2026-07-16; the identifier rename is an open decision for the Modes thread - if the id stays `deconstructing`, change it here too and keep the display name.

roles.research_note: Real query data: people ask about lived practice, not doctrine - clothing, food, greetings, marriage, fasting. Every top query under 'why were early christians...' is persecution or accusation.

sets.title: An ordinary day
sets.orientation: What a week actually looked like - the room, the food, the work, the people.

questions.text: Walk me through an ordinary day among your people - from waking to sleeping.
What did you eat, and who ate with you?
Would I have picked you out in a crowd, or did you look like everyone else?
What did people do for work - and did belonging to you change it?
What happened in a household once the day was over?

sets.title: The table you gathered at
sets.orientation: The meal at the centre of the gathering - who came, who led, what it meant.

questions.text: When your people gathered, what actually happened in the room?
Tell me about the meal you shared. Why did it matter so much?
Who led it - and how was that decided?
Was it done the same way everywhere, or differently in different places?
Was there anyone you wouldn't share it with?

sets.title: How you looked from outside
sets.orientation: What your neighbours thought you were - the rumours, the accusations, the danger.

questions.text: What did your neighbours think you were?
What were you accused of?
Was it dangerous to be what you were? What could actually happen, and who decided?
How did an ordinary person go about a week with that hanging over them?
Did it ever come near anyone you knew?

sets.title: Becoming one of you
sets.orientation: How someone joined - what they were taught, what changed, what it cost.

questions.text: How did someone become one of you?
What were they taught first - and why that first?
How long did it take, and who decided they were ready?
What changed for a person afterwards?
What did it cost them - with their family, their work, their old life?

sets.title: The argument you lived inside
sets.orientation: The question your people never settled, and how they stayed one people anyway.
sets.design_note: Offered to the general visitor deliberately, not held back as advanced material - Governance section 9 says hard questions are met at the level of the participant's need. This set is the direct answer to the sharpest external critique of AI historical figures: 'There are histories. There is no one narrative.'

questions.text: What did your people disagree about among themselves?
Did it ever come close to breaking you apart?
How did you stay one people with those who did it differently?
Did you expect it to be settled one day? Did you want it settled?
What would you say to someone who told you that you should all just agree?

roles.research_note: 87% of pastors use AI for research and raw material, 24% for authorship, 71% describe themselves as cautious. Every documented objection to canned material is an objection to a finished product replacing their own wrestling. Hand over the text, the voice, and the question - never the lesson. No question here names an application.

sets.title: Who led, and how that was decided
sets.orientation: Leadership as your people actually worked it out - offices, disputes, and what was never settled.

questions.text: Who led among your people - and how was that decided?
What did you call your leaders, and what did those words actually mean?
What happened when a leader failed, or was removed wrongly?
Did other communities do it differently? How did you regard them?
Which of your own writings would you put in my hands on this?

sets.title: Forming someone new
sets.orientation: How a person was taught, tested, and brought in - the practice behind the teaching.

questions.text: How did your people teach someone who was new?
What did you teach them first - and why that first?
Who did the teaching? Was it an office, or whoever could?
How did you know when someone was ready?
Is there a text you taught from that I could sit with myself?

sets.title: Failure, and what came after
sets.orientation: What your people did when someone fell - mercy, discipline, and the arguments about both.

questions.text: What happened among your people when someone failed badly?
Was there a way back? Who decided?
Did your people agree about that, or argue about it?
What did you do with someone who failed the same way again?
What did you say to the ones who were afraid they'd used up their chance?

sets.title: When you disagreed
sets.orientation: Conflict as your people actually handled it - the mechanics, not the ideal.

questions.text: What did your communities disagree about?
How did a disagreement actually get worked out - who spoke, who decided?
Did one community ever correct another? What happened?
What made an argument legitimate, and what made it a rupture?
Did any of it end badly?

sets.title: The texts you'd put in my hands
sets.orientation: The writings your people actually used, and what they were for.

questions.text: What did your people read when you gathered?
Where did those writings come from, and how did you get them?
How did you decide whether something could be trusted?
Which one would you hand to someone who teaches others?
What's in your writings that people misread?

roles.research_note: Built at the intersection of Paul's Socratic taxonomy and the historiographic probe register - structurally the same instrument. The register marker is that a probing question names its own defeasibility condition.

sets.title: How do you know that?
sets.orientation: The evidential standing of what you're being told, volunteered rather than extracted.

questions.text: How do your people know what you've told me - what stands behind it?
How much of what you know comes down through a single voice?
Where does documentation end and inference begin for you?
What in your own record is disputed - its dating, its authorship, whether it's genuine?
What would have to be true for you to be wrong about it - and would we be able to tell?

sets.title: Whose voice is this?
sets.orientation: Who wrote your record, who didn't, and what that does to what survives.

questions.text: Who among your people could write?
Whose voices are missing from your record entirely?
What do you know about those people, and how do you know it?
Does anything survive written by them, or only written about them?
What would you not claim to know about them?

sets.title: What you argued about
sets.orientation: The disagreements inside your own community - the evidence that this is a world, not a position.

questions.text: What did your people genuinely disagree about among themselves?
Was there a settled answer by the end of your time?
Who held each side, and what did each argue from?
Did either side treat the other as outside the faith?
Is there an argument your record preserves only one side of?

sets.title: Where your record thins
sets.orientation: The shape of the silences, and what kind of silence each one is.
sets.design_note: Q2 and Q3 hold apart two answers that are easy to conflate: 'we have no evidence of it' versus 'the category did not exist for them'. Conflating them implies a world should have had our category and merely failed to record it - Skinner's mythology of doctrines, committed by us, inside the set built to be honest about silence. Q3 is the one question in this curriculum that tests our framing rather than the world's.

questions.text: Where is your record thinnest?
Is that because nothing was written, or because nothing survived?
Is there something I've been asking about that your people wouldn't have recognised as a question at all?
What do people assume about your world that your record can't actually support?
What has been dug up from your world, and what hasn't?

sets.title: The contested ground
sets.orientation: Where your world's own material is disputed, and how you hold that.

questions.text: What in your record do people who study you fight about?
Is there something attributed to your people that they didn't actually say?
What in your tradition's memory of itself might be later polish?
Where does your world's account of itself flatter it?
What's the strongest case against how you've just described yourselves?

roles.research_note: The mechanism: a pre-offered hard question costs the participant no standing to ask. Where spiritual and epistemic credibility are fused, the act of asking lowers your standing to ask - so the house asking first is the whole point. Governing constraint: testimony, not argument. The world is allowed to be what it was; the walk is not allowed to aim it.

sets.title: Did any of you ever want to leave?
sets.orientation: Whether anyone in your world wanted out - asked of them, answered as testimony.

questions.text: Did any of you ever want to leave?
What was that like from the inside, for the ones who felt it?
Could they say it out loud? To whom?
Did anyone actually go? What did the rest of you say about them?
What kept the ones who stayed - honestly?

sets.title: When it went wrong among you
sets.orientation: Your world's own failures, named by it rather than about it.
sets.routing_note: Q5 routes, in the Syriac world, to the anti-Jewish polemic - that world's genuinely hardest true thing about itself, and the material its own brief calls the most sensitive in the record, recommended for external scholarly review before wide deployment. This is a per-world ANSWER, not a per-world question: the caution belongs in that world's coverage card, not as a hole in this curriculum.

questions.text: What went wrong among your people?
Did anyone get hurt by the way you did things?
Was there anything done in your name that you'd disown?
Did your people ever admit it - at the time, later, or never?
What's in your record that you're not proud of?

sets.title: Doubt, and whether there was room for it
sets.orientation: What your people did with someone who wasn't sure.

questions.text: Was there room among you for someone who doubted?
What did your people do with a person who wasn't sure?
Did anyone among you carry a doubt for years?
Was doubt treated as a failure, or as part of it?
Would there have been a place at your table for someone with more questions than answers?

sets.title: What you never settled
sets.orientation: The questions your world left open, held as they held them.
sets.design_note: The failure mode this set must not commit: if the cumulative weight says 'see, we were unsettled too, so it's fine', the walk has rebuilt the thought-terminating cliche out of historical material. The world's unsettledness is what was true of them, not what should settle the participant.

questions.text: What did your people never settle?
How did you live with it unsettled?
Did that trouble anyone, or was it just how things were?
How do you give your life to something that hasn't made up its mind about its own biggest questions?
Did you expect it to be settled? Did you want it to be?

sets.title: Say the hardest thing first
sets.orientation: The most honest thing your world can say about itself, offered first rather than last.
sets.design_note: Q5 is phrased about 'someone', not 'you', on purpose. The participant-framed version - 'if I walked away, what would you want to have told me?' - invites the Representative to make a case, which is a persuasion arc wearing an honesty costume. World-framed, it stays testimony.

questions.text: What's the hardest true thing about your people?
What would you rather I didn't know?
What did belonging actually cost among you?
Who paid for your way of life besides you?
If someone left your community for good, what would you have wanted them to know?
